error_modes.label: Lateral separation from the leading aircraft

texts.0: SP, due to an unstabilized aileron and rudder input on the roll-in, did not hold the 10 ft reference of lateral separation required in the echelon position. Wingtip spacing opened beyond 60 ft on the first turn and, on the reversal, closed inside the 10 ft reference so that the minimum safe distance was no longer protected. The excursion also exceeded the 1.5 wing span limit set by the general criteria. IP took control to re-establish lateral spacing before the maneuver was continued.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed lateral correction as the leader increased bank, allowed the wingtip spacing to reach approximately 60 ft, at the outer edge of the acceptable band. The wide position was held through most of the turn and was reduced only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. SP did not return to the 10 ft reference before the leader rolled out.
texts.2: SP, due to an over-controlled initial correction on the roll-in, opened lateral separation to approximately 35 ft from the 10 ft reference. SP recognized the widening sight picture without prompting and closed back toward the reference with a smooth aileron and power input before the leader rolled out. The deviation stayed inside the acceptable band throughout and no intervention was required.
texts.3: SP held lateral separation between 10 and 18 ft from the leading aircraft throughout the turn, keeping the wingtip spacing well inside 1.5 wing spans. Corrections were made with small aileron inputs as soon as the sight picture changed, so the position was re-established quickly. The reference distance was protected at every bank angle flown by the leader.
texts.4: SP maintained lateral separation within a few feet of the 10 ft reference for the whole turn, with no closure inside the reference at any point. Changes in the leader's bank produced only momentary spacing changes that SP removed immediately. The echelon geometry remained visibly constant from roll-in to roll-out.
texts.marginal: SP kept lateral separation inside the required limits, but worked consistently at the wide side of the band, around 18 to 20 ft, rather than at the 10 ft reference. The tendency to drift wide appeared each time the leader increased bank and was corrected late. SP is expected to fly closer to the reference distance and to remove the drift as it develops.

texts_at.0: SP flew the echelon position with the IP calling out the wingtip reference against the leader's wing, since the lateral picture for this position has not yet been built independently. This happens because the aileron correction on the roll-in is still sized for the steepest bank rather than the bank actually flown. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to scale the initial correction to the bank being flown so the spacing settles closer to the reference.
texts_at.1: SP held lateral separation to about 50 ft beyond the 10 ft reference on each turn, working the wide edge of the acceptable band rather than the reference itself. The margin stayed wide because the aileron correction on the roll-in is still sized for the steepest bank rather than the bank actually flown. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to scale the initial correction to the bank being flown so the spacing settles closer to the reference.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the widening wingtip picture without prompting on every turn and closed lateral separation to about 30 ft beyond the 10 ft reference before the leader rolled out. The correction was sized correctly but was started only once the gap had already opened rather than as it began to open. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin the correction at the first change in the sight picture rather than after it is established.
texts_at.3: SP held lateral separation no more than 10 ft wide of the 10 ft reference throughout the turn, keeping the wingtip spacing steady at every bank angle flown by the leader. The one small widening that appeared followed a coarse aileron input rather than a late one. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to soften the initial aileron input so the small excursion stops appearing at all.

texts_above.1: SP held lateral separation to about 45 ft beyond the 10 ft minimum through the turn, working the wide edge of the acceptable band. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized each widening of the wingtip picture without prompting and held lateral separation to about 30 ft beyond the 10 ft minimum, well inside the acceptable band for this turn. Reducing the size of the initial aileron correction on the roll-in would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good lateral spacing control.
texts_above.3: SP held lateral separation within about 8 ft of the 10 ft minimum through every bank angle flown, closing the wingtip picture with small, early aileron inputs rather than one late one. The reference distance was protected on both the roll-in and the reversal without a single wide excursion. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good lateral spacing control.
texts_above.4: SP kept the wingtip spacing within a foot or two of the 10 ft minimum for the whole turn, with no closure inside the reference at any bank angle flown. The echelon geometry looked fixed to the leader from roll-in through roll-out. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent lateral spacing control.

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient back pressure as bank was increased toward 60 degrees, did not hold the vertical position on the leading aircraft. SP descended more than 10 ft below the reference line and, after an abrupt recovery input, climbed above it by a similar amount, flying well outside the midpoint of the leader's wing. The vertical excursion exceeded the acceptable band in both directions. IP intervened to stop the climb toward the leader's flight path.
texts.1: SP, due to a late back pressure input on the roll-in, sank to approximately 10 ft below the reference, at the limit of the acceptable band. SP remained low on the leader's wing for most of the turn and started to recover only after the IP called the low position. The correct vertical reference was regained only near roll-out.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow pitch response to the leader's increasing bank, dropped approximately 7 ft below the reference line during the roll-in. SP saw the change against the leader's wing and restored the vertical position with a smooth back pressure input before the turn was established. The deviation remained inside the acceptable band and required no intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained vertical separation within 4 ft of the reference throughout the echelon turn, staying level with the midpoint of the leader's wing. Pitch corrections were small and applied as soon as the sight picture changed, so no vertical drift was allowed to build. The position was held through both the roll-in and the roll-out.
texts.4: SP held the vertical reference almost exactly on the midpoint of the leader's wing for the whole turn, with deviations barely perceptible from the cockpit. Increases in the leader's bank produced no visible sink or climb. The vertical geometry of the echelon was preserved without any noticeable correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept vertical separation within standards but showed a repeated tendency to settle low on the leader's wing, close to 4 ft below the reference, each time bank was increased. The corrections that followed were correct but late, so the low position persisted for several seconds per turn. SP is expected to anticipate the required back pressure and hold the midpoint reference more consistently.

texts_at.0: SP held a position under the leader's wing with the IP describing the midpoint reference through each turn, since the vertical picture has not yet been introduced independently. This happens because back pressure is still applied as a single input at the roll-in rather than fed in with the increasing bank. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to feed in back pressure progressively with the bank so the sink stays closer to the midpoint reference.
texts_at.1: SP held vertical separation to about 10 ft below the reference on each turn, staying at the upper edge of the acceptable band rather than at the midpoint of the leader's wing. The position sank that far because back pressure is still applied as a single input at the roll-in rather than fed in with the increasing bank. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to feed in back pressure progressively with the bank so the sink stays closer to the midpoint reference.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the low position without prompting on every turn and restored vertical separation to about 7 ft below the reference before the leader rolled out. The correction was applied correctly but only after the sink had already reached the middle of the band rather than as it began. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the back pressure correction at the first indication of sink rather than after it is established.
texts_at.3: SP held vertical separation within about 4 ft of the reference throughout the turn, staying close to the midpoint of the leader's wing at every bank angle flown. The small excursion that did appear followed a slightly late back pressure input on the steepest part of the turn. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lead the back pressure with the bank so the small sink no longer appears.

texts_above.1: SP held vertical separation to about 9 ft below the reference through the turn, staying at the upper edge of the acceptable band. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the developing sink on every turn without prompting and held vertical separation to about 7 ft below the reference, comfortably inside the acceptable band. Feeding back pressure in with the bank rather than after it starts to increase would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound vertical stack discipline.
texts_above.3: SP held vertical separation within about 3 ft of the reference at every bank angle flown, keeping the midpoint of the leader's wing in view without a late correction. The small excursions that did appear were removed before the next bank change developed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed vertical stack discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the vertical reference within about a foot of the midpoint of the leader's wing for the whole turn, with no sink or climb large enough to require a correction. The echelon geometry stayed visually constant through the steepest bank flown. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional vertical stack discipline.

error_modes.label: Longitudinal separation / fore-aft line on the leader

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated power management through the turn, did not hold the fore-aft line on the leading aircraft. SP moved forward past the leading edge of the leader's wing by more than 10 ft, then fell aft of the trailing edge of the stabilator after a large power reduction. Both excursions were outside the acceptable band and outside the reference points defined by the criteria. IP took control to stop the forward movement toward the leader.
texts.1: SP, due to a late throttle response as the leader rolled into the turn, went aft to approximately 10 ft, at the limit of the acceptable band, and remained sucked behind the reference line for most of the turn. The position was corrected only after the IP called for power. SP had not re-established the correct fore-aft line by roll-out.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly excessive power reduction on the roll-in, moved approximately 7 ft aft of the reference line on the leader. SP recognized the changing sight picture without prompting, added power early and returned to the correct fore-aft position before the turn was established. The deviation stayed inside the acceptable band and no intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP held longitudinal separation within 4 ft of the reference line throughout the turn, remaining between the leading edge of the wing and the trailing edge of the stabilator at all times. Power was adjusted promptly as the leader's bank changed, so no forward or aft drift was allowed to develop. The fore-aft position was stable through roll-in and roll-out.
texts.4: SP maintained the fore-aft line on the leading aircraft with deviations that were barely detectable against the reference points. Throttle inputs were anticipatory and continuous, so the echelon position showed no fore-aft movement even at the highest bank flown. The line was preserved throughout the maneuver.
texts.marginal: SP kept longitudinal separation within standards but sat repeatedly toward the aft side of the band, around 4 ft behind the reference, whenever the leader increased bank. The recovery to the correct line was made with a single large power input rather than a continuous adjustment. SP is expected to anticipate the power requirement and hold the fore-aft line with smaller inputs.

texts_at.0: SP held a position behind the leader with the IP pointing out the leading edge of the wing and the trailing edge of the stabilator, since the fore-aft references have not yet been introduced independently. This happens because the power reduction on the roll-in is still applied as one setting rather than matched to the changing bank. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to vary power with the bank so the aft slip stays closer to the reference line.
texts_at.1: SP held the fore-aft line to about 10 ft behind the leader on each turn, working the outer edge of the acceptable band rather than the reference line itself. The position slipped that far because the power reduction on the roll-in is still applied as one setting rather than matched to the changing bank. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to vary power with the bank so the aft slip stays closer to the reference line.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the aft drift without prompting on every turn and closed the fore-aft line to about 7 ft behind the leader before the reversal. The correction was sized correctly but was applied only after the drift had reached the middle of the band rather than at its start. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to add power at the first sign of the drift rather than once it is established.
texts_at.3: SP held the fore-aft line within about 4 ft of the reference throughout the turn, staying between the leading edge of the wing and the trailing edge of the stabilator at every bank flown. The small drift that did appear followed a slightly late power addition on the steepest part of the turn. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lead the power change with the bank so the small drift stops appearing.

texts_above.1: SP held the fore-aft line to about 9 ft aft of the leader through the turn, working the outer edge of the acceptable band. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the aft drift on every turn without prompting and closed the fore-aft line to about 7 ft aft of the leader, comfortably inside the acceptable band. Matching the power change to the bank rather than to the developing drift would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid longitudinal spacing control.
texts_above.3: SP held the fore-aft line within about 3 ft of the reference at every bank angle flown, adjusting power in small, early amounts rather than in a single late correction. No forward or aft drift was allowed to develop past that margin on any turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed longitudinal spacing control.
texts_above.4: SP held the fore-aft line within about a foot of the reference for the whole turn, with throttle inputs anticipatory enough that no drift became visible against the wing and stabilator references. The line was preserved through both the roll-in and the roll-out. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding longitudinal spacing control.

error_modes.label: Smooth and solid aircraft control in the echelon position

texts.0: SP, due to overcontrol in roll and pitch while attempting to hold position, did not control the aircraft in a smooth and solid way as No2. Inputs were large and alternating, producing an oscillation in all three axes that made the echelon position divergent rather than convergent. The oscillation carried the aircraft outside the acceptable separation band in more than one axis. IP took control to stabilize the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a stiff grip and stepped control inputs, flew the echelon turn with visible oscillation about the reference position and reached about 10 ft, the limit of the acceptable band, on each swing. The technique was changed to smaller, continuous inputs only after repeated verbal instruction from the IP. The aircraft was still not solidly stabilized in position by the end of the maneuver.
texts.2: SP, due to control inputs that were initially larger than required, produced a noticeable wallowing about the reference position, reaching about 7 ft off it during the roll-in. SP recognized the overcontrol without prompting, reduced the size of the inputs and settled the aircraft inside the acceptable band before the turn was established. The remainder of the turn was flown without intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way throughout the echelon turn, using small continuous inputs in roll, pitch and power. Corrections were applied in time and stopped on reaching the reference, with no overshoot, and all separations stayed inside the tightest band. The position looked stable from entry to recovery.
texts.4: SP flew the echelon turn with control inputs that were continuous and almost imperceptible, holding the position as if the aircraft were mechanically fixed to the leader. No overshoot or hunting was present in any axis at any bank angle. The aircraft remained solid in position from roll-in to roll-out.
texts.marginal: SP controlled the aircraft within standards, but the inputs were still made in discrete steps rather than as continuous pressures, which produced a small hunting motion about the reference position. The technique held the deviations inside limits without ever settling the aircraft fully. SP is expected to fly with smaller, blended inputs so that the position stops moving between corrections.

texts_at.0: SP flew the echelon position with the IP calling for smaller, continuous inputs each time the aircraft began to wallow, since smooth control of this position has not yet been practiced. This happens because the control inputs are still applied in discrete steps rather than as continuous pressure. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to blend the inputs into continuous pressure so the swing stays closer to the reference.
texts_at.1: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth way overall, but the position still oscillated to about 10 ft from the reference on each swing before settling, at the outer edge of the acceptable band. The swing reached that far because the control inputs are still applied in discrete steps rather than as continuous pressure. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to blend the inputs into continuous pressure so the swing stays closer to the reference.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the overcontrol without prompting on each turn and reduced the inputs before the position moved past about 7 ft from the reference. The correction was applied correctly but only once the wallowing motion was already visible rather than as it began. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce the size of the initial input so the wallowing motion does not develop at all.
texts_at.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way throughout the echelon turn, with any excursion held inside about 4 ft of the reference at every bank angle flown. The small excursions that did appear followed an input that was fractionally larger than required. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to size the initial input more finely so the small excursions stop appearing.

texts_above.1: SP controlled the aircraft with an oscillation about the reference position that reached about 9 ft before settling, at the outer edge of the acceptable band. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the beginning of each wallowing motion without prompting and held the aircraft within about 7 ft of the reference position, comfortably inside the acceptable band. Sizing the initial input to the bank actually being flown, rather than to the steepest bank of the set, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady aircraft control in the echelon position.
texts_above.3: SP controlled the aircraft with small, continuous inputs in roll, pitch and power throughout the turn, holding every excursion inside about 3 ft of the reference. Corrections stopped exactly on reaching the reference, with no overshoot on any bank angle flown. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate aircraft control in the echelon position.
texts_above.4: SP flew the echelon turn with inputs so continuous that the position never moved more than about a foot from the reference at any bank angle. No hunting or overshoot was present in any axis from roll-in to roll-out. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary aircraft control in the echelon position.

error_modes.label: Timeliness of corrections and arrest of developing drift

texts.0: SP, due to failure to trap a deviation that had already been detected, did not make the appropriate corrections in time as No2. A drift that started small was allowed to run until the aircraft was outside the acceptable band in lateral and vertical separation at the same time. The correction, when finally applied, was large enough to produce a second excursion in the opposite direction. IP intervened to recover the echelon position.
texts.1: SP, due to no mitigation applied after the deviation was recognized, allowed the position error to grow to the limit of the acceptable band before acting. The correction was started only after the IP prompted it verbally, and it was completed after the leader had already rolled out. SP treated each deviation as an event to be fixed later rather than immediately.
texts.2: SP, due to a short delay between recognizing the changed sight picture and acting on it, allowed the position to move to the middle of the acceptable band. SP then applied the correction without prompting and stopped the drift before it developed further. Recovery to the reference position was completed inside the turn and required no intervention.
texts.3: SP made the appropriate corrections in time throughout the echelon turn, acting on the first visible change in the sight picture rather than on an established error. Deviations were arrested while still inside the tightest band and were removed with a single input. No error was allowed to accumulate across the turn.
texts.4: SP anticipated the position changes associated with the leader's bank and applied the corrections before any deviation became measurable. Each input was matched to the requirement, so nothing had to be corrected twice. The echelon position never departed from the reference to a visible degree.
texts.marginal: SP corrected all deviations within standards, but the corrections were consistently started one or two seconds after the position had already moved, so the error was chased rather than prevented. The result stayed inside limits only because the initial deviations were small. SP is expected to act on the first change in the sight picture rather than on the established deviation.

texts_at.0: SP corrected each drift with the IP calling out the point at which the sight picture had changed, since detecting a developing deviation in this position has not yet been practiced. This happens because the correction is still triggered by the size of the error rather than by its onset. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to act at the first visible change in the sight picture so the arrest point moves back toward the reference.
texts_at.1: SP arrested each developing drift only once the position had reached about 10 ft from the reference, at the outer edge of the acceptable band, roughly two seconds after the sight picture had begun to change. The delay persisted because the correction is still triggered by the size of the error rather than by its onset. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to act at the first visible change in the sight picture so the arrest point moves back toward the reference.
texts_at.2: SP caught each drift at about 7 ft from the reference, roughly in the middle of the acceptable band, and applied the correction without prompting. The short delay before acting reflects a scan that confirms the trend before responding rather than reacting to the first indication. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to close that short confirmation delay so the drift is trapped nearer its onset.
texts_at.3: SP arrested drift while the position was still inside about 4 ft of the reference, acting on the first visible change rather than an established error. The small delay that remained came from a scan rate that checks the picture rather than holding it continuously. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the picture continuously so no delay is measurable at all.

texts_above.1: SP arrested each developing drift once the position had reached about 9 ft from the reference, at the outer edge of the acceptable band, roughly two seconds after the sight picture had begun to change. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP trapped every developing drift at about 7 ft from the reference, well inside the acceptable band, applying the correction without prompting each time. Holding the sight picture continuously rather than sampling it would close even that short recognition delay. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable correction timing.
texts_above.3: SP kept every drift inside about 3 ft of the reference by acting on the first visible change rather than the established error, with a single input removing each deviation before it could grow. No correction was left to accumulate across the turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good correction timing.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated each position change with the leader's bank and applied the correction before any deviation became measurable, so nothing was ever corrected twice. The echelon position never departed from the reference to a visible degree. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior correction timing.

error_modes.label: Visual cross-check on the leader and use of the sight picture

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted visual cross-check on the leading aircraft while attention shifted inside the cockpit, lost the reference points that define the echelon position. Without the wing and stabilator references, SP flew on bank angle alone and drifted outside the acceptable band in more than one axis. The deviation was not recognized until the geometry had changed substantially. IP intervened to re-establish the position and the outside reference.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check limited to one reference point on the leader, did not detect the developing vertical and fore-aft errors and reached the limit of the acceptable band. The full sight picture was resumed only after the IP described the reference points verbally. SP did not recover a stable scan of the leader before roll-out.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on lateral spacing at the expense of the other references, allowed the vertical position to move to the middle of the acceptable band. SP re-established the complete sight picture without prompting, identified the error against the leader's wing and corrected it inside the turn. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained a continuous visual cross-check on the leading aircraft, using the wing midpoint, the wing leading edge and the stabilator trailing edge as references. All three separations were assessed against the sight picture rather than against instruments, and deviations were kept inside the tightest band. The scan remained on the leader through the whole turn.
texts.4: SP used the full sight picture on the leading aircraft continuously and read every reference simultaneously, so any change in geometry was identified at the moment it began. The echelon position was flown entirely on outside references with negligible deviation in all three axes. The scan did not break at any point of the maneuver.
texts.marginal: SP kept the visual cross-check on the leader within acceptable standards, but the scan settled on the lateral reference and returned to the vertical and fore-aft references only intermittently. This produced late detection of small errors that remained inside limits. SP is expected to read all three references as a single sight picture rather than in sequence.

texts_at.0: SP flew the echelon position with the IP naming each of the three references in turn, since the full sight picture on the leader has not yet been built independently. This happens because the scan settled on the lateral picture and returned to the other two references late. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to cycle the scan through all three references rather than resting on one of them.
texts_at.1: SP's cross-check caught the vertical and fore-aft references only after they had drifted to about 10 ft from their marks, at the outer edge of the acceptable band, because the scan settled on the lateral picture and returned to the other two references late. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cycle the scan through all three references rather than resting on one of them.
texts_at.2: SP's scan picked up a vertical displacement at about 7 ft from the wing midpoint reference, inside the acceptable band, and the complete sight picture was re-established without prompting. The gap opened because the scan dwelt on lateral spacing before returning to the other references. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to shorten the interval between checks of the three references.
texts_at.3: SP's cross-check held every reference inside about 4 ft of its mark, reading the wing midpoint, the leading edge and the stabilator trailing edge as one continuous picture. The small excursions that did appear followed a scan that checks rather than holds the picture. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the full sight picture rather than sampling it in sequence.

texts_above.1: SP's cross-check caught the vertical and fore-aft references after they had drifted to about 9 ft from their marks, at the outer edge of the acceptable band. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP's cross-check kept every reference inside about 7 ft of its mark, comfortably within the acceptable band, by returning to the complete sight picture without prompting whenever the scan narrowed. Reading all three references as one picture rather than in sequence would tighten that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured cross-check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP read the wing midpoint, the leading edge and the stabilator trailing edge as a single continuous picture, holding every axis inside about 3 ft of its reference at every bank angle flown. The scan never narrowed to one reference at the expense of the others. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise cross-check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP read the full sight picture continuously and identified every change in geometry at the moment it began, with negligible deviation across all three axes for the whole turn. The scan did not break at any point of the maneuver. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate cross-check discipline.

error_modes.label: Safe distance and closure control at high bank
error_modes.source: general:a|conditions:pre-planned turns up to 60 degrees of bank

texts.0: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation as the leader rolled toward 60 degrees of bank, did not keep the required safe distance. Closure was allowed to develop toward the leading aircraft and the position came inside the 10 ft reference, with no margin remaining. SP did not call for separation or move away from the leader. IP took control to open the distance immediately.
texts.1: SP, due to a misjudged closure rate on the roll-in to the steepest turn, allowed the lateral position to move to the limit of the acceptable band and started to close toward the leader. The movement was stopped only after the IP called it, and no separation call was made by SP. Safe distance was preserved but with no margin created by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late assessment of closure as bank increased, allowed the lateral position to move within the acceptable band toward the leading aircraft. SP recognized the closure from the sight picture, stopped it with a positive input and re-established the reference distance without prompting. Safe distance was never in question and no intervention was required.
texts.3: SP kept a safe distance from the leading aircraft at every bank angle flown, holding the position inside the tightest band and never allowing closure inside the 10 ft reference. Closure rates were identified early from the sight picture and removed with small inputs. The wingtip spacing stayed well inside 1.5 wing spans throughout.
texts.4: SP controlled closure so precisely that the lateral spacing showed no perceptible change even during the roll into and out of the steepest turn. The reference distance was protected at all times with a clear margin and without any abrupt input. Safe separation from the leading aircraft was never approached.
texts.marginal: SP maintained safe distance within standards, but closure toward the leading aircraft was identified late on each roll-in and was stopped closer to the reference than intended. The margin remaining was small although the limits were respected. SP is expected to identify closure earlier and to build the correction before the spacing narrows.

texts_at.0: SP held position at high bank with the IP calling the closure rate as it developed, since judging closure against the leader has not yet been practiced independently. This happens because closure is still judged from the overall sight picture rather than from the changing rate as bank increases. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to read the closure rate earlier so the margin above the reference stays larger.
texts_at.1: SP stopped each closure before the 10 ft minimum was reached, but the correction left the spacing about 50 ft wide of the reference on the roll-in to the steepest turn, at the outer edge of the acceptable band. The margin swung that far because closure is still judged from the overall sight picture rather than from the changing rate as bank increases. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read the closure rate earlier so the correction stays smaller.
texts_at.2: SP identified the closure as bank increased and stopped it with a positive input that left the spacing about 30 ft wide of the reference, then closed back onto the echelon position without prompting. error_modes.label: Recognition that turns away from Number 2 are echelon in the recovery pattern
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, due to waiting for an echelon signal instead of applying the rule that all turns away from Number 2 inside the entry point are echelon unless briefed otherwise, held close references into the turn at pattern altitude. The aircraft finished the turn more than 10 ft out of the leader's plane of motion and with lateral spacing outside the acceptable band. The confusion persisted on the following turn in the pattern. IP took control to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to not applying the briefed rule for echelon turns during the recovery, entered the turn on close references and reached about 10 ft out of the plane of motion, at the limit of the acceptable band. The echelon position was established only after repeated verbal direction from the IP. SP required the same reminder before the next turn away.
texts.2: SP, due to a late recognition that the turn away at pattern altitude was to be flown as an echelon turn, spent the first part of the turn on close references and drifted about 7 ft out of the plane of motion. SP identified the error without prompting and re-established the echelon geometry before the rollout. The deviation stayed inside the acceptable band.
texts.3: SP applied the rule that turns away from Number 2 inside the entry point are echelon unless briefed otherwise and flew each pattern turn in the leader's plane of motion within 4 ft. The transition to the echelon position was made at the roll-in without prompting. Position was stable through the turns preceding the Break.
texts.4: SP treated every turn away from the formation in the recovery as an echelon turn without waiting for a signal, and held the plane of motion within one to two feet. The sight picture was established at the roll-in and remained unchanged through each turn. No prompting or clarification was required at any point of the recovery.
texts.marginal: SP flew the pattern turns inside the limits, but hesitated at each roll-in as if waiting for an echelon signal and let the displacement reach about 4 ft before settling into the echelon position. The hesitation was repeated on every turn away. SP is expected to apply the recovery rule for echelon turns without waiting for a signal.

texts_at.0: SP flew the pattern turns with the IP calling out that each turn away from Number 2 was to be flown as an echelon turn, since the recovery rule has not yet been applied without a reminder. This happens because the rule is still applied after a pause for confirmation rather than as the turn begins. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to apply the recovery rule for echelon turns at the start of the turn rather than after a pause.
texts_at.1: SP reached about 10 ft out of Number 1's plane of motion, at the limit of the acceptable band, before recognizing that the turn away at pattern altitude was to be flown in echelon. The displacement reached that far because the rule is still applied after a pause for confirmation rather than as the turn begins. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the recovery rule for echelon turns at the start of the turn rather than after a pause.
texts_at.2: SP spent the first part of the turn on close references and drifted about 7 ft out of the plane of motion, inside the acceptable band, before identifying the error without prompting and re-establishing the echelon geometry. The displacement reached that far because recognition of the recovery rule lagged the start of the turn by a moment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recognize the turn as echelon from the leader's initial roll rather than partway through it.
texts_at.3: SP flew each pattern turn in the leader's plane of motion within about 4 ft by applying the rule that turns away from Number 2 are echelon unless briefed otherwise. The small displacement that did appear followed a brief hesitation before the transition to the echelon position. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to remove that hesitation so the transition happens with the roll-in itself.

texts_above.1: SP reached about 9 ft out of Number 1's plane of motion, at the limit of the acceptable band, before recognizing that the turn away at pattern altitude was to be flown in echelon. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified each turn away as echelon and held displacement from the plane of motion to about 7 ft, comfortably inside the acceptable band, without waiting for a signal. Recognizing the turn from the leader's initial roll, rather than partway through it, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent recovery-turn recognition.
texts_above.3: SP applied the rule that turns away from Number 2 inside the entry point are echelon unless briefed otherwise and flew each pattern turn in the leader's plane of motion within about 4 ft, with the transition made at the roll-in without prompting. Position was stable through the turns preceding the Break. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined recovery-turn recognition.
texts_above.4: SP treated every turn away from the formation in the recovery as an echelon turn without waiting for a signal, holding the plane of motion within one to two feet, with the sight picture established at the roll-in and unchanged through each turn. No prompting or clarification was required at any point of the recovery. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless recovery-turn recognition.
